I will keep my farm centered on the wheat-maize rotation. In Quzhou County, that is still the most practical system for me because it fits the local climate, my equipment, and the way I spread risk across the year. At the start of this season, my winter wheat is already the backbone of my income, and after harvest I will follow immediately with summer maize on the same land. I have a high education level, so I prefer improved or hybrid seed, soil-tested fertilizer rates, and tighter field management instead of relying on habit alone. I will not scatter my land across too many crops, because that usually raises management complexity without improving whole-farm stability.

For winter wheat, I will push for a steady, high yield rather than the absolute maximum. I will use improved seed, balanced nitrogen with enough phosphorus and potassium, and several irrigations timed around key growth stages. I will control weeds and disease in a measured way, not by spraying excessively. After wheat harvest, I will plant hybrid summer maize quickly to protect yield from delayed sowing. I will keep fertilizer moderate but sufficient, use fewer irrigations than wheat because maize can tolerate short dry spells better, and I will watch pests closely during the humid summer period. For tillage, I will mainly use rotary tillage because it matches my machinery, helps me turn crops around fast between wheat and maize, and is a workable compromise between speed and soil preparation.
